prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

NEW YORK (CNN) -- Two customers are suing Wal-Mart for negligence after being injured in a mad rush for post-Thanksgiving bargains that left one store employee dead, the men's attorney said Tuesday. A temporary worker at this Wal-Mart was crushed to death when shoppers rushed into the store last week. Temporary Wal-Mart worker Jdimytai Damour, 34, was crushed to death as he and other employees attempted to unlock the doors of a store on Long Island at 5 a.m. Friday. Attorney Kenneth Mollins said Fritz Mesadieu and Jonathan Mesadieu were "literally carried from their position outside the store" and are now "suffering from pain in their neck and their back from being caught in that surge of people" that rushed into the Wal-Mart. New York Newsday reported that the Mesadieus are father and son, ages 51 and 19. The lawsuit alleges that the Mesadieus' injuries were a result of "carelessness, recklessness, negligence." In a claim against the Nassau County police department, the men also contend that they "sustained monetary losses as a result of health care and legal expenses ... in the sum of $2 million." "This is a tragic situation that could have and should have been avoided with the exercise of reasonable care. There are very simple measures that could have been put in place to avoid this, such as barriers along the line to spread people out, extra security and a better police presence," Mollins said. He said his clients and others who were at the scene contend that the police "were there ... saw what was happening, and they left." Calls seeking comment from Wal-Mart Stores Inc. were not immediately returned. Lt. Kevin Smith of the Nassau County Police Department said, "it's our policy that we don't comment on open litigations" and would not respond directly to Mollins and his clients' claim that officers left the scene. He said it is "incumbent upon the store to provide security" but noted that there was no security force present when officers responded to an initial phone call after 3 a.m. Friday for an unknown disturbance at the site. Smith said the officers noticed a lack of order with the crowd and began to organize them into a line, remaining on site for about 30 minutes until the crowd had become orderly. Throughout the morning, officers went back to check on the crowd and continued to notice no disturbance, Smith said. He said that there were no additional calls for assistance until about 5 a.m., when people began rushing the doors of the store and trampled Damour. An autopsy showed that Damour died of asphyxiation after being trampled, Nassau County officials have said. Video showed that as many as a dozen people were knocked to the floor in the stampede of people trying to get into the store. The employee was "stepped on by hundreds of people" as other workers attempted to fight their way through the crowd, said Nassau County Police Detective Lt. Michael Fleming. CNN's Kristen Hamill contributed to this report .

The fatality occurred at the same Wal-Mart last week, when a temporary employee was crushed as crowds forced their way inside. Officers later returned several times during the morning to check on the group and did not see any further problems, he said.

**NEW YORK** — Two Wal-Mart customers who say they were injured in the Black Friday crowd surge on Long Island that killed temporary worker Jdimytai Damour have filed a lawsuit against the retail giant, alleging the company failed to provide adequate security and crowd control for one of the busiest shopping days of the year.

Damour, 34, was trampled to death November 28 when hundreds of bargain-seeking shoppers forced their way through the doors of a Wal-Mart in Valley Stream, New York, shortly before the store’s early-morning opening. Several other people, including shoppers and employees, were injured in the chaos.

The lawsuit claims Wal-Mart knew or should have known that large crowds would gather outside the store and that the company did not take sufficient steps to prevent a dangerous rush when the doors opened. The plaintiffs say they suffered physical injuries when the crowd surged forward.

The suit also alleges negligence in the planning and management of the event, including inadequate barriers, staffing and emergency procedures.

Wal-Mart has previously said it cooperated with authorities after the incident and reviewed its safety procedures. The company also said at the time that it was saddened by Damour’s death.

The fatal stampede drew national attention to Black Friday crowd-control practices and raised questions about retailers’ responsibility to protect workers and customers during high-demand sales events.

Local officials said the crowd had been gathering for hours before the store opened. When the doors were unlocked, witnesses said shoppers pushed forward with such force that employees were knocked to the ground.

Damour, who had been hired as a seasonal worker, was pronounced dead at a hospital. His death was later ruled the result of asphyxiation caused by compression.

The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages.

**Lawsuit Filed After Deadly 2008 Wal-Mart Stampede in Valley Stream; Shoppers Say Store Failed to Control Black Friday Crowd**

**VALLEY STREAM, N.Y. —** A lawsuit has been filed in connection with the deadly Black Friday stampede at a Wal-Mart store in Nassau County, where a temporary employee was trampled to death and several shoppers were injured as crowds rushed the entrance before dawn.

The suit, brought on behalf of shoppers including **Fritz Mesadieu** and **Jonathan Mesadieu**, alleges that Wal-Mart failed to provide adequate security, crowd-control measures, and safe procedures for opening the store on one of the busiest shopping days of the year. Their attorney, **Kenneth Mollins**, said the chaos outside the Valley Stream location was foreseeable and preventable.

“This was not simply an accident,” Mollins said in announcing the legal action. “When a retailer advertises major holiday discounts and draws a massive crowd before sunrise, it has a responsibility to make sure customers and workers are protected.”

The lawsuit stems from the November 28, 2008 incident at the Wal-Mart on Green Acres Road, where hundreds of bargain-seekers gathered outside the store ahead of its scheduled Black Friday opening. As the doors opened, the crowd surged forward, knocking people to the ground and overwhelming workers at the entrance.

A 34-year-old temporary Wal-Mart employee, **Jdimytai Damour**, was fatally trampled. Other employees and customers were also hurt as the crowd pushed into the store. Witnesses described people screaming, falling, and being stepped on as shoppers continued moving toward sale items inside.

According to the allegations, Fritz and Jonathan Mesadieu were among those caught in the crush of people. The lawsuit claims they suffered physical injuries and emotional trauma as a result of the uncontrolled crowd and the store’s alleged failure to prepare for the expected rush.

Mollins said Wal-Mart should have used barriers, staggered entry, additional security, and clearer crowd-management procedures. He argued that the store had ample warning because Black Friday promotions routinely attract large crowds and because employees were reportedly concerned about the growing number of people outside before the doors opened.

**Nassau County police** responded to the scene after reports of injuries and disorder at the store. Officers and emergency personnel arrived to assist victims, control the crowd, and investigate the circumstances surrounding Damour’s death. Police said at the time that the situation involved an extremely large and aggressive crowd that surged forward when the doors opened.

The incident drew national attention and raised questions about retail safety practices during major holiday sales. Nassau County officials and investigators reviewed surveillance footage, witness accounts, and store procedures as part of the response.

Wal-Mart previously expressed condolences over Damour’s death and said it cooperated with authorities. The company also said it had taken steps to improve safety at high-traffic sales events. However, attorneys for injured shoppers and Damour’s family argued that those measures came too late.

The lawsuit seeks damages for injuries allegedly sustained during the stampede and contends that the store’s planning and security failures directly contributed to the dangerous conditions.

The Valley Stream stampede remains one of the most widely cited examples of Black Friday crowd-control failures in the United States, prompting retailers nationwide to rethink how they manage doorbuster sales, early openings, and large holiday crowds.
